title: The commute
hookLine: travel time can be practice time

cards: A train car in the morning, rows of heads bent over glowing screens. A line of cars at a red light. A bus window streaked with rain.
Between the start of the workday and its end there's a stretch that belongs to neither home nor work, and it's easy to treat it as time to be killed.

Henry David Thoreau, in his essay Walking, says he has met hardly anyone who understood the art of walking, who had, as he puts it, a genius for sauntering. Then he tells a story about where that word came from.

teach.b: He says saunter comes from idlers in the Middle Ages who roamed the country asking for charity on the pretense of going to the Holy Land, à la Sainte Terre, until children cried, there goes a Sainte-Terrer, a saunterer, a Holy-Lander.
Whether or not a dictionary agrees, his point is clear: a walk can be a small pilgrimage. Second, a psalm for the trip.

teach.h: THY GOING OUT AND COMING IN.
teach.b: In the King James Bible, Psalm 121 ends: "The LORD shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in from this time forth, and even for evermore." The whole commute fits in one line.
Third, a prayer for the road. Jewish tradition has Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, said when setting out on a journey, asking to be brought to the destination in peace and returned in peace.
The road itself is a place where something deserves to be said. Fourth, the steps.
In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha teaches that when walking, a practitioner knows, I am walking. Some Buddhists practice walking as a meditation of its own, attention resting in the feet.
So travel time can be practice time, though not every trip in the same way: a driver's practice is full attention on the road.

But a walk, a train, a bus, a passenger seat can be a stretch of quiet between the two halves of a day. This week ran through work's corners: envy, a difficult boss, mistakes, a craft, a beginning and an ending.
The commute is the road that connects them.

how: Jews say Tefilat HaDerech, the traveler's prayer, when setting out on a journey; some Buddhists practice walking meditation; Christians and Jews read Psalm 121 as a psalm for travelers.

o: the hours spent working from home each day
the daily trip between home and work, as practice
a long pilgrimage to a holy place far away

games.q: what's inside the road — tap the pairs.
p: thy going out and thy coming in

s: Thoreau links saunter to wanderers bound for the Holy Land
he says idlers who claimed to be going à la Sainte Terre were called Sainte-Terrers: saunterers.
Psalm 121 speaks only of setting out, not of returning
it names both: thy going out and thy coming in.
in the Satipatthana Sutta, walking is a time to let the mind wander
when walking, the practitioner knows, I am walking.

games.q: you're on foot, heading somewhere ordinary, with the phone in your pocket. Thoreau has one word for doing this well. which?
games.why: sauntering, which he traces, playfully, to Sainte-Terrers: travelers bound for the Holy Land.

practice: Picture the trip you make most often, and imagine making it once with the phone left in a pocket.

Let three things from the route come to mind, a tree, a corner, a face; if you drive, picture the road itself, held in full attention. If you pray, you can bring the going out and the coming in to God in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: The commute. The going out and the coming in, which can be practice time instead of time to be killed. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the prayer of the road, the traveler's prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: the road. A trip can be a small pilgrimage. That's the week, and day nine hundred twenty-four.
